  buffer size and character code is a bare number repeated wherever it is
  used. hlasm's `EQU` and expressions (`SIZE EQU WORDS*3`) are computed at
  assembly time and written into the output as numbers.
- **Repeated idioms.** Polling the UART, saving registers or setting up a
  call frame is the same 4-6 lines every time. A macro writes it once;
  `\@` gives each expansion its own labels, so loops inside macros work.
- **Branch spaghetti.** Hand-written `if`/`else` and loops need invented
  labels and inverted conditions. `IF`/`ELSE`/`ENDIF`, `DO`/`DOEXIT`/`ENDDO`
  and `SELECT`/`WHEN` read like the logic and generate the labels for you.
  COR24 branches only reach -128..127 bytes; hlasm measures its output and
  switches to a long-range jump automatically when a block is too big, so
  structured code never fails with "branch target too far".
- **One source, several builds.** `SET`/`IFDEF`/`IFEQ` select debug code,
  targets or features without editing the source.
- **Readable output.** The generated `.s` is ordinary COR24 assembly you can
  read, diff and debug; optional annotations mark where each structured
  statement came from.

A small example: print "Hi" on the UART.

```
; hello.hlasm: print "Hi" on the UART, then spin
UART EQU -65280

MACRO PUTC &CH
 lc r0,&CH
L\@:
 lb r1,1(r2)
 cls r1,z
 brt L\@
 sb r0,0(r2)
MEND

 la r2,UART
 PUTC 'H'
 PUTC 'i'
halt:
 bra halt
```

hlasm output (blank lines from the consumed `EQU`/`MACRO` lines trimmed):

```
; hello.hlasm: print "Hi" on the UART, then spin
 la r2,-65280
 lc r0,72
L0001:
 lb r1,1(r2)
 cls r1,z
 brt L0001
 sb r0,0(r2)
 lc r0,105
L0002:
 lb r1,1(r2)
 cls r1,z
 brt L0002
 sb r0,0(r2)
halt:
 bra halt
```

Assembled with `cor24-asm` and run on `cor24-emu`, it prints `Hi`. Each
further character is one line of source instead of six, and the UART
address and character codes are names instead of numbers.

## Setup

You need three tools; hlasm itself needs no build step.

| Tool | From | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| `cor24-asm` | [sw-cor24-x-assembler](https://github.com/sw-embed/sw-cor24-x-assembler) | assembling `hlasm.s` and hlasm's output |
| `cor24-emu` | [sw-cor24-emulator](https://github.com/sw-embed/sw-cor24-emulator) | running hlasm and the programs it produces |
| `reg-rs` | (test runner) | `./build.sh test` only |

`scripts/run-kernel.sh` finds `cor24-asm` and `cor24-emu` on `PATH`, through
`COR24_ASM` / `COR24_EMU`, or in sibling checkouts' `target/release`
directories (for example `../sw-cor24-x-assembler/target/release/cor24-asm`).
It assembles a `.s` file and runs it in one step; everything below uses it.

Quick checks:

```bash
./build.sh          # assemble hlasm.s (sanity check)
./demo.sh           # show a demo source, hlasm's output, and that it assembles
./build.sh test     # run the regression suite
```

## Running hlasm

hlasm reads its source from memory at address 0x080000 (524288), so a run has
three parts: turn the source into a loadable image, run hlasm on the emulator
with that image loaded, and keep the UART output.

```bash
# 1. Source text -> loadable image
bash demos/make_bin.sh prog.hlasm prog.bin

# 2. Run hlasm with the image at 0x080000; -q prints only the UART output
scripts/run-kernel.sh hlasm.s --load-binary prog.bin@524288 \
    --speed 0 -n 5000000 -q 2>/dev/null | grep -v '^Executed' > prog.s

# 3. Assemble and run the generated program
scripts/run-kernel.sh prog.s --speed 0 -n 100000
```

Notes:

- `-n` is the instruction budget for the emulator. hlasm costs roughly 10-15
  thousand instructions per source line (it makes two passes); give it
  plenty, it stops by itself when done. `--speed 0` runs at full speed.
- hlasm ends by spinning on `bra` to itself (how COR24 halts); `cor24-emu`
  detects this and stops.
- If hlasm stops with a line starting `ERROR:`, the source exceeded a limit
  or contains an error (see [Limits and error messages](#limits-and-error-messages)).
- The main source can be up to 32,767 bytes this way. Larger programs, or
  programs split into several files, use a source set
  ([INCLUDE and COPY](#multiple-source-files-include-and-copy)).

## Source format

- One statement per line, at most 256 characters.
- Lines starting with `;` are comments and are copied to the output.
- `name:` at the start of a line defines a label (passed to `cor24-asm`).
- Instructions are written as in COR24 assembly, conventionally indented by
  one space: ` add r0,1`.
- hlasm directives (`MACRO`, `SET`, `IF`, `DO`, ...) start in column 1 or
  after blanks and are upper case.
- Anything hlasm does not recognize is passed through unchanged, so any
  valid COR24 assembly is also valid hlasm source.

## Named constants: EQU and SET

```
name EQU expression
SET name,expression
```

Both define an assembly-time symbol with a 24-bit value. Names are up to 31
characters (letters, digits, `_`). `EQU` is the HLASM spelling for
constants; `SET` is used for values you redefine, such as configuration
switches.

Symbols are replaced by their values wherever a value is expected:

- operands of instructions, `.byte` and `.word`;
- compare values in `IF`, `ELSEIF`, `DOEXIT` and `WHEN`;
- `SET`, `EQU`, `IFEQ`, `IFNE`.

An operand is rewritten only if every name in it is a symbol and there is
something to compute; registers, labels and plain numbers are left for
`cor24-asm`. In a memory operand `offset(reg)` only the offset is rewritten.

```
WORDS EQU 4
SIZE EQU WORDS*3
FLAGS EQU (1<<4)|0x0F
SET LAST,SIZE-3
 lc r0,SIZE
 la r1,FLAGS
 lw r0,LAST(fp)
 lc r2,'A'+1
 .byte SIZE,FLAGS,'\n'
 .word SIZE*100
 la r0,buffer
```

Output:

```
 lc r0,12
 la r1,31
 lw r0,9(fp)
 lc r2,66
 .byte 12,31,10
 .word 1200
 la r0,buffer
```

`buffer` is a label, not a symbol, so `la r0,buffer` is left for
`cor24-asm`.

## Expressions

Expressions combine numbers, character literals and symbols:

| Precedence (high to low) | Operators |
|---|---|
| unary | `-x` `~x` `+x` |
| multiplicative | `*` `/` `%` |
| additive | `+` `-` |
| shift | `<<` `>>` |
| bitwise and | `&` |
| bitwise xor | `^` |
| bitwise or | `\|` |

- Parentheses group as usual.
- Numbers: decimal `42`, hex `0x2A` or `2Ah`, binary `0b101010`.
- Character literals: `'A'`, and escapes `'\n'` `'\t'` `'\r'` `'\0'` `'\\'`
  `'\''`.
- Arithmetic is 24-bit. `>>` is an arithmetic (sign-preserving) shift; `/`
  and `%` truncate toward zero, as in C (`-17/5` is `-3`).
- Division or remainder by zero stops with `ERROR: division by zero in
  expression`.
- Negative results are written as negative decimals (`lc r0,-3`), which
  `cor24-asm` accepts.

## Macros

```
MACRO name [&param1,&param2,...]
 body lines
MEND
```

A macro is invoked by writing its name as a statement, followed by
arguments separated by commas. Parameters are referred to by name (`&A`) or
by position (`&1` to `&9`):

```
MACRO PUSH2 &A,&B
 push &A
 push &B
MEND
MACRO POP2
 pop &2
 pop &1
MEND
 PUSH2 r0,r1
 POP2 r0,r1
```

Output:

```
 push r0
 push r1
 pop r1
 pop r0
```

- Up to 256 macros, names up to 31 characters, up to 16 named parameters
  with names up to 31 characters. All macro bodies together can use 64 KB.
- `\@` expands to a number unique to each expansion (`0001`, `0002`, ...),
  so a label like `L\@:` inside a macro is distinct every time the macro is
  used (see `PUTC` above).
- A missing argument expands to nothing.
- Symbols in a macro's output are substituted like any other line, so
  `PUTC 'H'` produces `lc r0,72`.
- Arguments are separated by commas; an argument ends at a comma, blank or
  end of line.

## Conditional assembly

Conditional assembly includes or skips source lines at assembly time:

```
SET DEBUG,1
SET LEVEL,2
IFDEF DEBUG
 nop
ENDIFASM
IFEQ LEVEL,3
 add r0,3
ELSEASM
 add r0,1
ENDIFASM
IFNDEF RELEASE
 lc r1,0
ENDIFASM
```

Output:

```
 nop
 add r0,1
 lc r1,0
```

| Directive | Includes the block when |
|---|---|
| `IFDEF name` | the symbol is defined and not 0 |
| `IFNDEF name` | the symbol is not defined |
| `IFEQ name,expr` | the symbol's value equals the expression |
| `IFNE name,expr` | the symbol's value differs from the expression |
| `ELSEASM` | the preceding condition was false |
| `ENDIFASM` | ends the block |

Blocks nest up to 32 deep.

## Structured control flow

Structured statements compare a register with a value and generate the
labels and branches. Conditions are written `cc, register, value`:

| Condition | True when |
|---|---|
| `cc_eq` | register = value |
| `cc_ne` | register != value |
| `cc_lt` | register < value (signed) |
| `cc_lu` | register < value (unsigned) |
| `cc_zset` | the C flag is set (no operands; test a compare you just did) |
| `cc_zclr` | the C flag is clear |

The value can be a register, a number, or a symbol expression. A constant is
loaded into a scratch register that is saved and restored around the
compare (`push r2` / `lc r2,...` / `pop r2`), so the generated code changes
no registers except the ones your own code changes.

### IF / ELSEIF / ELSE / ENDIF

```
LIMIT EQU 10
IF cc_lt, r0, LIMIT
 add r0,1
ELSE
 lc r0,0
ENDIF
```

Output:

```
 push r2
 lc r2,10
 cls r0,r2
 pop r2
 brt _hlif_3_skip
 bra _hlif_1_false
_hlif_3_skip:
 add r0,1
 bra _hlif_2_end
_hlif_1_false:
 lc r0,0
_hlif_2_end:
```

`ELSEIF cc, reg, value` adds further branches; `ELSE` is optional.

### DO / DOEXIT / ITERATE / ENDDO

`DO` ... `ENDDO` loops forever; `DOEXIT cc, reg, value` leaves the loop when
the condition is true, and `ITERATE` jumps back to the top.

```
 lc r0,0
DO
 add r0,1
 DOEXIT cc_eq, r0, 5
ENDDO
```

Output:

```
 lc r0,0
_hldo_1_top:
 add r0,1
 push r2
 lc r2,5
 ceq r0,r2
 pop r2
 brf _hldo_3_skip
 bra _hldo_2_end
_hldo_3_skip:
 bra _hldo_1_top
_hldo_2_end:
```

### SELECT / WHEN / OTHERWISE / ENDSEL

```
SELECT r0
WHEN 1
 lc r1,10
WHEN 2
 lc r1,20
OTHERWISE
 lc r1,0
ENDSEL
```

Each `WHEN value` arm runs when the selected register equals the value;
`OTHERWISE` runs when no arm matched.

### Nesting and long blocks

IF, DO and SELECT each nest up to 32 deep. Generated labels
(`_hlif_N_...`, `_hldo_N_...`, `_hlsel_N_...`) are unique across the whole
program, so avoid starting your own labels with `_hl`.

Every structured jump is emitted as `bra` when the target is within reach
and otherwise as `push r2` / `la r2,L_far` / `jmp (r2)` with a matching
`pop r2` at the target, so a block can be any size. hlasm decides this by
sizing its output in a first pass; nothing needs to be marked by hand.
Demo d40 shows the long form.

## Data directives

`.byte` and `.word` pass through (with symbols substituted). hlasm also
lowers these conveniences to `.byte` lists:

```
msg:
.asciz "Hi\n"
.ascii "\x41B"
.space 3
.fill 2,0x7F
```

Output:

```
msg:
.byte 72,105,10,0
.byte 65,66
.byte 0,0,0
.byte 127,127
```

| Directive | Produces |
|---|---|
| `.ascii "text"` | the characters |
| `.asciz "text"` | the characters and a terminating 0 |
| `.space n` | `n` zero bytes |
| `.fill n,v` | `n` bytes of value `v` |

String escapes: `\n` `\t` `\r` `\0` `\\` `\"` `\'` and `\xNN` (two hex
digits). Any other escape stops with `ERROR: unknown escape in string or
character literal`.

`cor24-asm` does not accept label arithmetic in `.word` (`.word msg+1`); use
a separate label instead.

## Multiple source files: INCLUDE and COPY

Larger programs are split into members: a main source plus named files that
the main source pulls in with `INCLUDE name` or `COPY name` (the HLASM
spelling, typically used for macro and symbol libraries). Members can
include other members, up to 8 deep.

The files are described by a **source set**, and
`reg-rs/run_bootstrap_sourceset.sh` builds the images, loads them and runs
hlasm:

```
# prog.sourceset
PROFILE default.profile
ROOT .
MAIN prog.hlasm
COPY libmac macros.hlasm
COPY libsym symbols.hlasm
```

```
; prog.hlasm
COPY libmac
COPY libsym
PUSH2 r0,r1
```

```bash
bash reg-rs/run_bootstrap_sourceset.sh prog.sourceset 5000000 -q
```

Source-set lines:

| Line | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `MAIN file.hlasm` | the main source |
| `INCLUDE name file` / `COPY name file` | a member available under `name` |
| `SOURCESET other.sourceset` | read another source set (for sharing member lists) |
| `PROFILE file` | read shared defaults (e.g. `demos/default.profile`) |
| `ROOT dir` | directory that file names are relative to |
| `MAINADDR` / `EXTRAADDR` / `ALIGN` | load addresses and alignment (rarely needed) |

A source set lifts the 32,767-byte main-source limit; together, all files
fit in the 256 KB window at 0x080000-0x0BFFFF. Today a source set can name
3 members, with names of up to 8 characters (see
[Not supported yet](#not-supported-yet)). Demos d23, d24 and d34 show
complete source sets.

## Listings, cross-reference and diagnostics

Four switches add information to the output as `;` comments, so the result
still assembles. Each is turned on by `SET name,1` anywhere in the source:

| Switch | Adds |
|---|---|
| `HLANN` | `; HLASM IF ...` / `; HLASM THEN` / `; HLASM ENDIF` markers around structured code |
| `HLIST` | lines for each `COPY`, macro definition, macro expansion and `EQU` |
| `HLXREF` | a cross-reference at the end: members copied, macros defined and how often each was expanded, symbols |
| `HLDIAG` | warnings such as unknown mnemonics and undefined symbols, with source and line |

Annotated structured code (`SET HLANN,1`):

```
; HLASM IF cc_eq, r0, 0
 push r2
 lc r2,0
 ceq r0,r2
 pop r2
 brt _hlif_3_skip
 bra _hlif_1_false
_hlif_3_skip:
; HLASM THEN
 add r1,1
_hlif_1_false:
_hlif_2_end:
; HLASM ENDIF
```

A diagnostic (`SET HLDIAG,1`, then `SET RESULT,FLAG+UNDEF`):

```
; !! hlasm: HLDIAG active at src0:5
; !! hlasm: undefined symbol 'UNDEF' at src0:5
```

A cross-reference (`SET HLXREF,1`):

```
; HLASM XREF BEGIN
; HLASM XREF COPY libmac
; HLASM XREF MACRO PUSH2
; HLASM XREF EXPAND PUSH2 1
; HLASM XREF END
```

## Limits and error messages

hlasm checks every limit. Exceeding one stops hlasm with a single `ERROR:`
line; nothing is silently truncated.

| Item | Limit | Error |
|---|---|---|
| Source line | 256 characters | `input line longer than 256 characters` |
| Symbols | 512 | `symbol table overflow (512 symbols)` |
| Symbol name | 31 characters | `symbol name longer than 31 characters` |
| Macros | 256 | `macro table overflow (256 macros)` |
| Macro name | 31 characters | `macro name longer than 31 characters` |
| Macro parameters | 16 | `more than 16 macro parameters` |
| Parameter name | 31 characters | `macro parameter name longer than 31 characters` |
| All macro bodies | 64 KB | `macro body pool overflow (65536 bytes)` |
| Expanded macro line | 256 characters | `expanded macro line longer than 256 characters` |
| Conditional nesting | 32 | `conditional assembly nested deeper than 32` |
| IF / DO / SELECT nesting | 32 each | `IF nested deeper than 32` (and DO, SELECT) |
| Division | non-zero divisor | `division by zero in expression` |
| String escapes | see above | `unknown escape in string or character literal` |

For example, `SET THIS_NAME_IS_MUCH_TOO_LONG_FOR_HLASM,1` gives:

```
ERROR: symbol name longer than 31 characters
```

Values are 24-bit and wrap like COR24 arithmetic. Structured labels and
`\@` numbers have no practical limit.

## Not supported yet

These are planned (see `docs/limits-and-lifting-plan.md` for the schedule):

- **Macros calling macros, and directives inside macro bodies.** A macro
  body is expanded as text: a macro name or `IF`/`IFDEF` inside a body is
  copied to the output rather than processed.
- **Default and keyword parameters** (`&V=5`, `NAME=value`).
- **More include members**: a source set can name 3 members with names of
  up to 8 characters, and error messages do not yet name the member and
  line.
- **Compound conditions** (`IF cc_eq,r0,1,AND,...`) and record layouts
  (`DSECT`).
- **Labels as values.** Labels are resolved by `cor24-asm`, not hlasm, so
  they cannot be used in `EQU`, `SET` or conditions.

## Further reading

- `demos/README.md`: the demo programs (d01-d41) and what each shows.
- `docs/design.md`: the language design and lowering rules.
- `docs/limits-and-lifting-plan.md`: every limit, known issue and the plan
  for lifting the rest.
- `docs/structured-jump-relaxation.md`: how long-range structured jumps work.
- `docs/architecture.md`: hlasm's internals and memory layout.

# hlasm User Guide

hlasm is a macro assembler for the COR24 24-bit RISC CPU, modelled on IBM's
High Level Assembler (HLASM). You write `.hlasm` source with macros, named
constants, expressions, conditional assembly and structured control flow
(IF / DO / SELECT); hlasm turns it into plain COR24 assembly (`.s`) that
`cor24-asm` assembles and `cor24-emu` (or the FPGA) runs.

hlasm is itself a COR24 program (`hlasm.s`), so it runs on the emulator
like any other COR24 code: the source is loaded into memory and the
generated assembly comes out of the UART.

Every example in this guide was run through hlasm; the outputs shown are
what it printed.

- [Why use hlasm](#why-use-hlasm)
- [Setup](#setup)
- [Running hlasm](#running-hlasm)

- [Macros](#macros)
- [Conditional assembly](#conditional-assembly)
- [Structured control flow](#structured-control-flow)
- [Data directives](#data-directives)
- [Multiple source files: INCLUDE and COPY](#multiple-source-files-include-and-copy)
- [Listings, cross-reference and diagnostics](#listings-cross-reference-and-diagnostics)
- [Limits and error messages](#limits-and-error-messages)
- [Not supported yet](#not-supported-yet)

Plain COR24 assembly makes you do by hand what a macro assembler does for
you:

- **No named constants.** `cor24-asm` has no `EQU`, so every UART address,
  buffer size and character code is a bare number repeated wherever it is
  used. hlasm's `EQU` and expressions (`SIZE EQU WORDS*3`) are computed at
  assembly time and written into the output as numbers.
- **Repeated idioms.** Polling the UART, saving registers or setting up a
  call frame is the same 4-6 lines every time. A macro writes it once;
  `\@` gives each expansion its own labels, so loops inside macros work.
- **Branch spaghetti.** Hand-written `if`/`else` and loops need invented
  labels and inverted conditions. `IF`/`ELSE`/`ENDIF`, `DO`/`DOEXIT`/`ENDDO`
  and `SELECT`/`WHEN` read like the logic and generate the labels for you.
  COR24 branches only reach -128..127 bytes; hlasm measures its output and
  switches to a long-range jump automatically when a block is too big, so
  structured code never fails with "branch target too far".

  read, diff and debug; optional annotations mark where each structured
  statement came from.

```

 sb r0,0(r2)
MEND

 bra halt
```

 cls r1,z
 brt L0001
 sb r0,0(r2)

Symbols are replaced by their values wherever a value is expected:

- operands of instructions, `.byte` and `.word`;
- compare values in `IF`, `ELSEIF`, `DOEXIT` and `WHEN`;
- `SET`, `EQU`, `IFEQ`, `IFNE`.

An operand is rewritten only if every name in it is a symbol and there is
something to compute; registers, labels and plain numbers are left for
`cor24-asm`. In a memory operand `offset(reg)` only the offset is rewritten.

```
WORDS EQU 4
SIZE EQU WORDS*3
FLAGS EQU (1<<4)|0x0F
SET LAST,SIZE-3
 lc r0,SIZE
 la r1,FLAGS
 lw r0,LAST(fp)
 lc r2,'A'+1
 .byte SIZE,FLAGS,'\n'
 .word SIZE*100
 la r0,buffer
```

Output:

```
 lc r0,12
 la r1,31
 lw r0,9(fp)
 lc r2,66
 .byte 12,31,10
 .word 1200
 la r0,buffer
```

`buffer` is a label, not a symbol, so `la r0,buffer` is left for
`cor24-asm`.

## Expressions

Expressions combine numbers, character literals and symbols:

| Precedence (high to low) | Operators |
|---|---|
| unary | `-x` `~x` `+x` |
| multiplicative | `*` `/` `%` |
| additive | `+` `-` |
| shift | `<<` `>>` |
| bitwise and | `&` |
| bitwise xor | `^` |
| bitwise or | `\|` |

- Parentheses group as usual.
- Numbers: decimal `42`, hex `0x2A` or `2Ah`, binary `0b101010`.
- Character literals: `'A'`, and escapes `'\n'` `'\t'` `'\r'` `'\0'` `'\\'`
  `'\''`.
- Arithmetic is 24-bit. `>>` is an arithmetic (sign-preserving) shift; `/`
  and `%` truncate toward zero, as in C (`-17/5` is `-3`).
- Division or remainder by zero stops with `ERROR: division by zero in
  expression`.
- Negative results are written as negative decimals (`lc r0,-3`), which
  `cor24-asm` accepts.

## Macros

```
MACRO name [&param1,&param2,...]
 body lines
MEND
```

A macro is invoked by writing its name as a statement, followed by
arguments separated by commas. Parameters are referred to by name (`&A`) or
by position (`&1` to `&9`):

```
MACRO PUSH2 &A,&B
 push &A
 push &B
MEND
MACRO POP2
 pop &2
 pop &1
MEND
 PUSH2 r0,r1
 POP2 r0,r1
```

Output:

```
 push r0
 push r1
 pop r1
 pop r0
```

- Up to 256 macros, names up to 31 characters, up to 16 named parameters
  with names up to 31 characters. All macro bodies together can use 64 KB.
- `\@` expands to a number unique to each expansion (`0001`, `0002`, ...),
  so a label like `L\@:` inside a macro is distinct every time the macro is
  used (see `PUTC` above).
- A missing argument expands to nothing.
- Symbols in a macro's output are substituted like any other line, so
  `PUTC 'H'` produces `lc r0,72`.
- Arguments are separated by commas; an argument ends at a comma, blank or
  end of line.

## Conditional assembly

Conditional assembly includes or skips source lines at assembly time:

```
SET DEBUG,1
SET LEVEL,2
IFDEF DEBUG
 nop
ENDIFASM
IFEQ LEVEL,3
 add r0,3
ELSEASM
 add r0,1
ENDIFASM
IFNDEF RELEASE
 lc r1,0
ENDIFASM
```

Output:

```
 nop
 add r0,1
 lc r1,0
```

| Directive | Includes the block when |
|---|---|
| `IFDEF name` | the symbol is defined and not 0 |
| `IFNDEF name` | the symbol is not defined |
| `IFEQ name,expr` | the symbol's value equals the expression |
| `IFNE name,expr` | the symbol's value differs from the expression |
| `ELSEASM` | the preceding condition was false |
| `ENDIFASM` | ends the block |

Blocks nest up to 32 deep.

## Structured control flow

Structured statements compare a register with a value and generate the
labels and branches. Conditions are written `cc, register, value`:

| Condition | True when |
|---|---|
| `cc_eq` | register = value |
| `cc_ne` | register != value |
| `cc_lt` | register < value (signed) |
| `cc_lu` | register < value (unsigned) |
| `cc_zset` | the C flag is set (no operands; test a compare you just did) |
| `cc_zclr` | the C flag is clear |

The value can be a register, a number, or a symbol expression. A constant is
loaded into a scratch register that is saved and restored around the
compare (`push r2` / `lc r2,...` / `pop r2`), so the generated code changes
no registers except the ones your own code changes.

### IF / ELSEIF / ELSE / ENDIF

```
LIMIT EQU 10
IF cc_lt, r0, LIMIT
 add r0,1
ELSE
 lc r0,0
ENDIF
```

Output:

```
 push r2
 lc r2,10
 cls r0,r2
 pop r2
 brt _hlif_3_skip
 bra _hlif_1_false
_hlif_3_skip:
 add r0,1
 bra _hlif_2_end
_hlif_1_false:
 lc r0,0
_hlif_2_end:
```

`ELSEIF cc, reg, value` adds further branches; `ELSE` is optional.

### DO / DOEXIT / ITERATE / ENDDO

`DO` ... `ENDDO` loops forever; `DOEXIT cc, reg, value` leaves the loop when
the condition is true, and `ITERATE` jumps back to the top.

```
 lc r0,0
DO
 add r0,1
 DOEXIT cc_eq, r0, 5
ENDDO
```

Output:

```
 lc r0,0
_hldo_1_top:
 add r0,1
 push r2
 lc r2,5
 ceq r0,r2
 pop r2
 brf _hldo_3_skip
 bra _hldo_2_end
_hldo_3_skip:
 bra _hldo_1_top
_hldo_2_end:
```

### SELECT / WHEN / OTHERWISE / ENDSEL

```
SELECT r0
WHEN 1
 lc r1,10
WHEN 2
 lc r1,20
OTHERWISE
 lc r1,0
ENDSEL
```

Each `WHEN value` arm runs when the selected register equals the value;
`OTHERWISE` runs when no arm matched.

### Nesting and long blocks

IF, DO and SELECT each nest up to 32 deep. Generated labels
(`_hlif_N_...`, `_hldo_N_...`, `_hlsel_N_...`) are unique across the whole
program, so avoid starting your own labels with `_hl`.

Every structured jump is emitted as `bra` when the target is within reach
and otherwise as `push r2` / `la r2,L_far` / `jmp (r2)` with a matching
`pop r2` at the target, so a block can be any size. hlasm decides this by
sizing its output in a first pass; nothing needs to be marked by hand.
Demo d40 shows the long form.

## Data directives

`.byte` and `.word` pass through (with symbols substituted). hlasm also
lowers these conveniences to `.byte` lists:

```
msg:
.asciz "Hi\n"
.ascii "\x41B"
.space 3
.fill 2,0x7F
```

Output:

```
msg:
.byte 72,105,10,0
.byte 65,66
.byte 0,0,0
.byte 127,127
```

| Directive | Produces |
|---|---|
| `.ascii "text"` | the characters |
| `.asciz "text"` | the characters and a terminating 0 |
| `.space n` | `n` zero bytes |
| `.fill n,v` | `n` bytes of value `v` |

String escapes: `\n` `\t` `\r` `\0` `\\` `\"` `\'` and `\xNN` (two hex
digits). Any other escape stops with `ERROR: unknown escape in string or
character literal`.

`cor24-asm` does not accept label arithmetic in `.word` (`.word msg+1`); use
a separate label instead.

## Multiple source files: INCLUDE and COPY

Larger programs are split into members: a main source plus named files that
the main source pulls in with `INCLUDE name` or `COPY name` (the HLASM
spelling, typically used for macro and symbol libraries). Members can
include other members, up to 8 deep.

The files are described by a **source set**, and
`reg-rs/run_bootstrap_sourceset.sh` builds the images, loads them and runs
hlasm:

```
# prog.sourceset
PROFILE default.profile
ROOT .
MAIN prog.hlasm
COPY libmac macros.hlasm
COPY libsym symbols.hlasm
```

```
; prog.hlasm
COPY libmac
COPY libsym
PUSH2 r0,r1
```

```bash
bash reg-rs/run_bootstrap_sourceset.sh prog.sourceset 5000000 -q
```

Source-set lines:

| Line | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `MAIN file.hlasm` | the main source |
| `INCLUDE name file` / `COPY name file` | a member available under `name` |
| `SOURCESET other.sourceset` | read another source set (for sharing member lists) |
| `PROFILE file` | read shared defaults (e.g. `demos/default.profile`) |
| `ROOT dir` | directory that file names are relative to |
| `MAINADDR` / `EXTRAADDR` / `ALIGN` | load addresses and alignment (rarely needed) |

A source set lifts the 32,767-byte main-source limit; together, all files
fit in the 256 KB window at 0x080000-0x0BFFFF. Today a source set can name
3 members, with names of up to 8 characters (see
[Not supported yet](#not-supported-yet)). Demos d23, d24 and d34 show
complete source sets.

## Listings, cross-reference and diagnostics

Four switches add information to the output as `;` comments, so the result
still assembles. Each is turned on by `SET name,1` anywhere in the source:

| Switch | Adds |
|---|---|
| `HLANN` | `; HLASM IF ...` / `; HLASM THEN` / `; HLASM ENDIF` markers around structured code |
| `HLIST` | lines for each `COPY`, macro definition, macro expansion and `EQU` |
| `HLXREF` | a cross-reference at the end: members copied, macros defined and how often each was expanded, symbols |
| `HLDIAG` | warnings such as unknown mnemonics and undefined symbols, with source and line |

Annotated structured code (`SET HLANN,1`):

```
; HLASM IF cc_eq, r0, 0
 push r2
 lc r2,0
 ceq r0,r2
 pop r2
 brt _hlif_3_skip
 bra _hlif_1_false
_hlif_3_skip:
; HLASM THEN
 add r1,1
_hlif_1_false:
_hlif_2_end:
; HLASM ENDIF
```

A diagnostic (`SET HLDIAG,1`, then `SET RESULT,FLAG+UNDEF`):

```
; !! hlasm: HLDIAG active at src0:5
; !! hlasm: undefined symbol 'UNDEF' at src0:5
```

A cross-reference (`SET HLXREF,1`):

```
; HLASM XREF BEGIN
; HLASM XREF COPY libmac
; HLASM XREF MACRO PUSH2
; HLASM XREF EXPAND PUSH2 1
; HLASM XREF END
```

## Limits and error messages

hlasm checks every limit. Exceeding one stops hlasm with a single `ERROR:`
line; nothing is silently truncated.

| Item | Limit | Error |
|---|---|---|
| Source line | 256 characters | `input line longer than 256 characters` |
| Symbols | 512 | `symbol table overflow (512 symbols)` |
| Symbol name | 31 characters | `symbol name longer than 31 characters` |
| Macros | 256 | `macro table overflow (256 macros)` |
| Macro name | 31 characters | `macro name longer than 31 characters` |
| Macro parameters | 16 | `more than 16 macro parameters` |
| Parameter name | 31 characters | `macro parameter name longer than 31 characters` |
| All macro bodies | 64 KB | `macro body pool overflow (65536 bytes)` |
| Expanded macro line | 256 characters | `expanded macro line longer than 256 characters` |
| Conditional nesting | 32 | `conditional assembly nested deeper than 32` |
| IF / DO / SELECT nesting | 32 each | `IF nested deeper than 32` (and DO, SELECT) |
| Division | non-zero divisor | `division by zero in expression` |
| String escapes | see above | `unknown escape in string or character literal` |

For example, `SET THIS_NAME_IS_MUCH_TOO_LONG_FOR_HLASM,1` gives:

```
ERROR: symbol name longer than 31 characters
```

Values are 24-bit and wrap like COR24 arithmetic. Structured labels and
`\@` numbers have no practical limit.

## Not supported yet

These are planned (see `docs/limits-and-lifting-plan.md` for the schedule):

- **Macros calling macros, and directives inside macro bodies.** A macro
  body is expanded as text: a macro name or `IF`/`IFDEF` inside a body is
  copied to the output rather than processed.
- **Default and keyword parameters** (`&V=5`, `NAME=value`).
- **More include members**: a source set can name 3 members with names of
  up to 8 characters, and error messages do not yet name the member and
  line.
- **Compound conditions** (`IF cc_eq,r0,1,AND,...`) and record layouts
  (`DSECT`).
- **Labels as values.** Labels are resolved by `cor24-asm`, not hlasm, so
  they cannot be used in `EQU`, `SET` or conditions.

## Further reading

- `demos/README.md`: the demo programs (d01-d41) and what each shows.
- `docs/design.md`: the language design and lowering rules.
- `docs/limits-and-lifting-plan.md`: every limit, known issue and the plan
  for lifting the rest.
- `docs/structured-jump-relaxation.md`: how long-range structured jumps work.
- `docs/architecture.md`: hlasm's internals and memory layout.

content.text:
Step 5 and the user guide are done and pushed (0d2becd); 67/67 tests pass. Now your question.

## How close is self-hosting?

`docs/bootstrap-hlasm.md` lists seven things that must be fixed before hlasm can assemble a full HLASM rewrite of itself. Five are done; two remain, and those are the next two saga steps.

| Prerequisite | Status |
|---|---|
| Lowering bugs (DOEXIT, `ceq`, `0b`) | done (step 3) |
| Symbol and macro tables big enough for hlasm-sized code, with no silent overflow | done (step 4) |
| Structured label and jump tables (4,096 entries) | done (step 4) |
| Line-length errors | done (step 4) |
| Source capacity | mostly done: a source set can feed hlasm a main file of any size within the 256 KB window. Splitting the 159 KB source into ~15–25 files needs more than today's 3 include slots → step 7 |
| Macros the rewrite relies on: macros calling macros, directives (`IFDEF`/`IF`/`SET`) inside macro bodies, default parameters | step 6, still to do |
| Error messages that name the file and line (`ERROR: <member>:<line>: ...`) | step 7, still to do |

## How much more work in hand-written assembly?

Two steps, 6 and 7, before hlasm has everything the self-hosting saga needs:

- **Step 6, macro layering, is the big one.** Today an expanded macro line goes straight to the output. It has to be fed back through the normal line processor, with a stack of active expansions, so nested calls and directives inside bodies work. It's a change to the core loop, likely at least the size of step 4's table work.
- **Step 7, include capacity and error locations, is moderate.** A new config-block layout with 32 slots and 15-character names (hlasm plus the sourceset tools), deeper include nesting, and tracking the current file and line for error messages.

# HLASM Macro-Assembler Demos

Each demo is a self-contained `.hlasm` source file showing one or more features.
Use `make_bin.sh` to convert `.hlasm` to `.bin` for loading into the emulator.

## Feature Status

| d01 | Basic passthrough | WORKS |
| d02 | Simple macro (no params) | WORKS |

| d24 | Nested named includes | WORKS |

| d32 | Literals and data ergonomics | WORKS |

| d34 | COPY macro library workflow | WORKS |
| d35 | Listing/xref comments | WORKS |
| d36 | End-of-run HLXREF report | WORKS |
| d36 | IF/ELSEIF/ENDIF without ELSE | WORKS |
| d37 | HLDIAG diagnostic baseline | WORKS |
| d38 | HLDIAG unknown mnemonic | WORKS |

| d40 | Long-range structured jumps (far form + trampoline) | WORKS |
| d41 | EQU constants, expressions, symbols in operands (prints CA4Y2! when run) | WORKS |

## Demo Policy

Every new HLASM feature or bootstrap milestone should add:

- one source demo
- one `reg-rs` regression test
- one README status entry

## Running a Demo

```bash
# Convert source to binary
bash demos/make_bin.sh demos/d01_passthrough.hlasm demos/d01_passthrough.bin

# Run on emulator
scripts/run-kernel.sh hlasm.s --load-binary demos/d01_passthrough.bin@524288 --speed 0 -n 100000 2>&1
```

## HLASM Syntax Reference

### Macros

Current supported baseline:

- `MACRO name` starts a definition and `MEND` ends it
- definition lines are consumed by the assembler and are not emitted to output
- simple no-parameter invocations expand stably
- positional parameters `&1`, `&2`, ... expand stably
- HLASM-style named parameters `&name` in both the definition header and body
  expand stably
- macro names up to 31 characters are supported
- multi-macro/local-label robustness is not complete yet
- macro bodies are plain text expansion; conditional-assembly directives and
  structured control-flow keywords are supported as top-level source forms,
  not as reparsed directives nested inside macro bodies

```
MACRO name
 <body>
MEND
<name>              ; invoke macro
```

This repo is aiming toward HLASM-like behavior on the MVS lineage, but the
currently implemented macro subset is still narrower than full HLASM macro
semantics.

Named parameters:
```
MACRO PUSH2 &LEFT,&RIGHT
 push &LEFT
 push &RIGHT
MEND
PUSH2 r0,r1
```

Positional parameters:
```
MACRO PUSH2
 push &1
 push &2
MEND
PUSH2 r0,r1
```

### Conditional Assembly (SET / IFDEF / IFNDEF / IFEQ / IFNE / ELSEASM / ENDIFASM)

```
SET DEBUG,1         ; define symbol DEBUG = 1

IFDEF DEBUG         ; include if DEBUG is defined
 nop
ENDIFASM

IFNDEF RELEASE      ; include if RELEASE is NOT defined
 nop
ENDIFASM

IFEQ VER,3          ; include if VER equals 3
 nop
ELSEASM             ; otherwise include this block
 add r0,1
ENDIFASM

IFNE VER,2          ; include if VER does NOT equal 2
 sub r0,1
ENDIFASM
```

Assembly-time numeric literals accepted by `SET`, `IFEQ`, `IFNE`, and
structured compare lowering:
```
SET COUNT,42
SET MASK,0x2A
SET BITS,0b101010
SET SAME,2Ah
```

Assembly-time expressions (`| ^ & << >> + - * / %`, unary `- ~`, parentheses,
character literals; see docs/user-guide.md) work in `SET`, `EQU`,
`IFEQ`, `IFNE`, structured compares, and instruction/.byte/.word operands,
where symbol expressions are replaced by their decimal values (demo d41):
```
MASK EQU 0x20
STEP EQU 2
SET BASE,8
SET TOTL,MASK+BASE+STEP
IFEQ TOTL,42
 nop
ENDIFASM
```

Current-location and label arithmetic remain assembler passthrough, not
assembly-time evaluation inside `hlasm`:
```
mark:
 .word mark+3
 .word tail-mark
tail:
```

### Data Directives

Current practical data-directive conveniences:

- `.ascii "text"` lowers to a `.byte` list
- `.asciz "text"` lowers to a `.byte` list with trailing `0`
- `.space N` lowers to `N` zero bytes
- `.fill N,V` lowers to `N` copies of byte value `V`

Examples:
```
.ascii "HI\n"
.asciz "OK"
.space 4
.fill 3,0x7F
```

### Source Buffer Control

```
SRCBUF 1            ; jump directly to preloaded source slot 1

INCBUF 1            ; push current slot/position, read slot 1, then
                    ; return to the caller source when slot 1 hits EOF

INCLUDE tail        ; resolve "tail" through the low-SRAM include-name table,
                    ; then include that slot and resume the caller source

COPY libmac         ; HLASM-style alias for a named source member, useful
                    ; for macro and symbol library fragments
```

Bootstrap-facing include demos and proofs now use a source-set manifest:
optional `PROFILE file`, then `ROOT dir`, optional `MAINADDR` / `EXTRAADDR` /
`ALIGN`, `SOURCESET child.sourceset`, then `MAIN file.hlasm` plus repeated
`INCLUDE name file.hlasm` or `COPY name file.hlasm`. The host-side runner
builds the `.bin` files, packs include buffers from their real sizes, emits the
unchanged low-SRAM config image, and feeds the same runtime include table into
`hlasm.s`.

Demo 34 uses the same composed source-set path to package a small copied macro
library plus a copied symbol library, then consumes both from a main source via
`COPY`.

Demo 24 now uses that composed source-set path directly, so the fragment model
is exercised on a named-include proof as well as the split `hlasm0` bootstrap
proof.

Demo 23 now uses the same composed source-set path, so both named-include
proofs run through the shared demo profile and fragment workflow.

Conditionals can nest:
```
SET OUTER,1
SET INNER,0
IFDEF OUTER
 IFDEF INNER
  add r0,1
 ELSEASM
  nop
 ENDIFASM
ELSEASM
 sub r0,1
ENDIFASM
```

### Structured Control Flow

#### IF / ELSEIF / ELSE / ENDIF
Nested `IF` blocks and `ELSEIF` chains now lower to plain labels and branches.
Structured conditionals are emitted in a long-range-safe form: a short
reversed conditional branch skips over an unconditional transfer, so generated
control flow does not depend on raw `bra` reach. The transfer is `bra L`
when its worst-case offset fits; otherwise it is `push r2` / `la r2,L_far` /
`jmp (r2)`, and the target gets a `bra L` / `L_far:` / `pop r2` trampoline
(see docs/structured-jump-relaxation.md; hlasm sizes its output in a first
pass to decide).
When `SET HLANN,1` is active, `hlasm` also emits opt-in semicolon comment
lines that mark structured source boundaries in the lowered `.s` output.

When `SET HLIST,1` is active, `hlasm` emits broader listing/xref-friendly
semicolon comments for consumed source-level events such as:

- `COPY name`
- `MACRO name`
- `EXPAND name`
- `EQU name`

`HLIST` is intended for understanding generated assembly and expansion flow.
`HLANN` remains the narrower switch for structured-control-flow source markers.
They can be used independently.
`HLXREF` is a separate opt-in switch for a compact end-of-run cross-reference
section.

When `SET HLXREF,1` is active, `hlasm` emits a compact end-of-run section:

```asm
; HLASM XREF BEGIN
; HLASM XREF COPY libmac
; HLASM XREF MACRO PUSH2
; HLASM XREF EXPAND PUSH2 1
; HLASM XREF SYMBOL LOCAL
; HLASM XREF END
```

```
IF cc_eq, r0, 0
    add r1,1
    IF cc_ne, r1, z
        lc r0,0
    ELSEIF cc_lt, r2, 10
        add r2,1
    ELSE
        nop
    ENDIF
ELSEIF cc_zclr
    add r0,1
ELSE
    add r2,2
ENDIF
```
Condition codes: cc_eq, cc_ne, cc_lt (signed), cc_lu (unsigned),
cc_zset (C flag set), cc_zclr (C flag clear).

Annotation example:
```
SET HLANN,1
IF cc_eq, r0, 0
    add r1,1
ENDIF
```

This emits normal lowered assembly plus comment markers such as:
```
; HLASM IF cc_eq, r0, 0
; HLASM THEN
; HLASM ENDIF
```

#### DO / DOEXIT / ITERATE / ENDDO
Loop lowering uses the same long-range-safe pattern for generated exits and
back-edges, with unconditional structured transfers relaxed the same way.

```
DO
    add r0,1
    DOEXIT cc_eq, r0, 10
    nop
ENDDO
DO
    add r1,1
    ITERATE
ENDDO
```

#### SELECT / WHEN / OTHERWISE / ENDSEL
```
SELECT r0
    WHEN 0
        add r1,1
    WHEN 1
        add r2,1
    OTHERWISE
        lc r1,0
ENDSEL
```

### Passthrough

Any line that is not a directive, macro definition, or structured keyword
is emitted unchanged. This includes labels, instructions, and comment lines.

### Labels
```
mylabel:
 bra mylabel
```

71	## HLASM Syntax Reference
72	
73	### Macros
74	
75	Current supported baseline:
76	
77	- `MACRO name` starts a definition and `MEND` ends it
78	- definition lines are consumed by the assembler and are not emitted to output
79	- simple no-parameter invocations expand stably

86	  structured control-flow keywords are supported as top-level source forms,

92	MEND

97	currently implemented macro subset is still narrower than full HLASM macro
98	semantics.

104	 push &RIGHT
105	MEND
106	PUSH2 r0,r1

108

111	MACRO PUSH2
112	 push &1
113	 push &2
114	MEND
115	PUSH2 r0,r1
116	```
117	
118	### Conditional Assembly (SET / IFDEF / IFNDEF / IFEQ / IFNE / ELSEASM / ENDIFASM)
119	
120	```
121	SET DEBUG,1         ; define symbol DEBUG = 1
122	
123	IFDEF DEBUG         ; include if DEBUG is defined
124	 nop
125	ENDIFASM
126	
127	IFNDEF RELEASE      ; include if RELEASE is NOT defined
128	 nop
129	ENDIFASM
130	
131	IFEQ VER,3          ; include if VER equals 3
132	 nop
133	ELSEASM             ; otherwise include this block
134	 add r0,1
135	ENDIFASM
136	
137	IFNE VER,2          ; include if VER does NOT equal 2
138	 sub r0,1
139	ENDIFASM
140	```
141	
142	Assembly-time numeric literals accepted by `SET`, `IFEQ`, `IFNE`, and
143	structured compare lowering:
144	```
145	SET COUNT,42
146	SET MASK,0x2A
147	SET BITS,0b101010
148	SET SAME,2Ah
149	```
150	
151	Assembly-time expressions (`| ^ & << >> + - * / %`, unary `- ~`, parentheses,
152	character literals; see docs/user-guide.md) work in `SET`, `EQU`,
153	`IFEQ`, `IFNE`, structured compares, and instruction/.byte/.word operands,
154	where symbol expressions are replaced by their decimal values (demo d41):
155	```
156	MASK EQU 0x20
157	STEP EQU 2
158	SET BASE,8
159	SET TOTL,MASK+BASE+STEP
160	IFEQ TOTL,42
161	 nop
162	ENDIFASM
163	```
164	
165	Current-location and label arithmetic remain assembler passthrough, not
166	assembly-time evaluation inside `hlasm`:
167	```
168	mark:
169	 .word mark+3
170	 .word tail-mark
171	tail:
172	```
173	
174	### Data Directives
175	
176	Current practical data-directive conveniences:
177	
178	- `.ascii "text"` lowers to a `.byte` list
179	- `.asciz "text"` lowers to a `.byte` list with trailing `0`
180	- `.space N` lowers to `N` zero bytes
181	- `.fill N,V` lowers to `N` copies of byte value `V`
182	
183	Examples:
184	```
185	.ascii "HI\n"
186	.asciz "OK"
187	.space 4
188	.fill 3,0x7F
189	```
190	
191	### Source Buffer Control
192	
193	```
194	SRCBUF 1            ; jump directly to preloaded source slot 1
195	
196	INCBUF 1            ; push current slot/position, read slot 1, then
197	                    ; return to the caller source when slot 1 hits EOF
198	
199	INCLUDE tail        ; resolve "tail" through the low-SRAM include-name table,
200	                    ; then include that slot and resume the caller source
201	
202	COPY libmac         ; HLASM-style alias for a named source member, useful
203	                    ; for macro and symbol library fragments
204	```
205	
206	Bootstrap-facing include demos and proofs now use a source-set manifest:
207	optional `PROFILE file`, then `ROOT dir`, optional `MAINADDR` / `EXTRAADDR` /
208	`ALIGN`, `SOURCESET child.sourceset`, then `MAIN file.hlasm` plus repeated
209	`INCLUDE name file.hlasm` or `COPY name file.hlasm`. The host-side runner
210	builds the `.bin` files, packs include buffers from their real sizes, emits the
211	unchanged low-SRAM config image, and feeds the same runtime include table into
212	`hlasm.s`.

215	library plus a copied symbol library, then consumes both from a main source via
216	`COPY`.

219	is exercised on a named-include proof as well as the split `hlasm0` bootstrap
220	proof.
221	
222	Demo 23 now uses the same composed source-set path, so both named-include
223	proofs run through the shared demo profile and fragment workflow.
224

226	```
227	SET OUTER,1
228	SET INNER,0
229	IFDEF OUTER
230	 IFDEF INNER
231	  add r0,1
232	 ELSEASM
233	  nop
234	 ENDIFASM
235	ELSEASM
236	 sub r0,1
237	ENDIFASM
238	```

240	### Structured Control Flow
241	
242	#### IF / ELSEIF / ELSE / ENDIF
243	Nested `IF` blocks and `ELSEIF` chains now lower to plain labels and branches.
244	Structured conditionals are emitted in a long-range-safe form: a short
245	reversed conditional branch skips over an unconditional transfer, so generated
246	control flow does not depend on raw `bra` reach. The transfer is `bra L`
247	when its worst-case offset fits; otherwise it is `push r2` / `la r2,L_far` /
248	`jmp (r2)`, and the target gets a `bra L` / `L_far:` / `pop r2` trampoline
249	(see docs/structured-jump-relaxation.md; hlasm sizes its output in a first
250	pass to decide).
251	When `SET HLANN,1` is active, `hlasm` also emits opt-in semicolon comment
252	lines that mark structured source boundaries in the lowered `.s` output.
253	
254	When `SET HLIST,1` is active, `hlasm` emits broader listing/xref-friendly
255	semicolon comments for consumed source-level events such as:
256	
257	- `COPY name`
258	- `MACRO name`
259	- `EXPAND name`
260	- `EQU name`
261	
262	`HLIST` is intended for understanding generated assembly and expansion flow.
263	`HLANN` remains the narrower switch for structured-control-flow source markers.
264	They can be used independently.
265	`HLXREF` is a separate opt-in switch for a compact end-of-run cross-reference
266	section.
267	
268	When `SET HLXREF,1` is active, `hlasm` emits a compact end-of-run section:

272	; HLASM XREF COPY libmac
273	; HLASM XREF MACRO PUSH2
274	; HLASM XREF EXPAND PUSH2 1

276	; HLASM XREF END
277	```

283	        lc r0,0
284	    ELSEIF cc_lt, r2, 10
285	        add r2,1
286	    ELSE
287	        nop
288	    ENDIF

291	ELSE
292	    add r2,2
293	ENDIF
294	```

311	```

333	        add r1,1

335	        add r2,1

338	ENDSEL
339	```

; Demo 41: EQU constants, expressions, and symbols in operands.
; cor24-asm has no EQU, so hlasm replaces symbol expressions in instruction,
; .byte and .word operands (and in IF/DOEXIT/WHEN compares) with decimal
; values. Labels and registers are left for cor24-asm. Assembled and run on
; cor24-emu this prints "CA4Y2!" (see hlasm_d41_equ_and_expressions_run).
UART EQU -65280
CH_A EQU 'A'
STEP EQU 3*4-10
MASK EQU (1<<4)|0x0F
HALF EQU 100/7
REM EQU 100%7
NEG EQU -17/5
INV EQU ~0&0xFF
BIG EQU 1000
OFFS EQU 6
SET COUNT,STEP+1

MACRO PUTC &R
L\@:
 lb r1,1(r2)
 cls r1,z
 brt L\@
 sb &R,OFFS-6(r2)
MEND

 la r2,UART
 lc r0,CH_A+STEP
 PUTC r0
 lc r0,0
DO
 add r0,1
 DOEXIT cc_eq, r0, COUNT
ENDDO
SELECT r0
WHEN COUNT
 lc r0,CH_A
OTHERWISE
 lc r0,'?'
ENDSEL
 PUTC r0
 lc r0,'0'+HALF-10
 PUTC r0
 la r1,BIG
IF cc_eq, r1, BIG
 lc r0,'Y'
ELSE
 lc r0,'N'
ENDIF
 PUTC r0
 lc r0,'5'+NEG
 PUTC r0
 la r0,msg
 lb r0,2(r0)
 PUTC r0
halt:
 bra halt

table:
 .byte STEP,CH_A,MASK,INV,REM
 .word BIG*2,msg
msg:
.asciz "hi\x21"

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. ## claude-artifacts
Claude may publish its own work without being asked, because artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared further: anything that imitates a real organization, person or record, and anything the person presented as sensitive. Claude builds those as files and lets the person decide whether they get a URL. When a finished piece of work is meant for other people or agents, such as a report for a team or the case for a decision the team has yet to make, Claude does not treat it as finished while it exists only in this conversation or in a local file. Claude publishes it and gives the person the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose. Claude publishes it even when the request is phrased as a question, such as "can you write up the plan?". When the request says who else will read or use the work, such as a team, a manager or a reviewer, or where it will be posted or presented, such as a channel or a meeting, Claude publishes it. A recommendation or analysis written up for someone else to act on is finished work for that reader, so Claude publishes it. Call guide before the first publish of a session: it holds the rules a page must meet. This server cannot change who can see an artifact (sharing, publishing to the web, unsharing), delete an artifact or read view counts; say so instead of calling a tool. # Personal instructions

## Python
- Never use the system `python3` (Xcode/Homebrew/user-site) for anything: not for running
  project code, scratch experiments, or one-off text edits.
- Always create the environment with `uv venv` and install packages with `uv pip install ...`.
- Run Python via `.venv/bin/python` (or `uv run`). If `.venv` is missing, create it first.

# AGENTS.md

## Baseline expectations for agentrail-driven sessions

You are working with the agentrail saga/steps process. The saga record (the
`.agentrail/` directory) is the durable handoff between sessions — if your
work is not reflected there, the next session cannot see it.

Before reporting work as complete:

- Confirm the active step is reflected in `.agentrail/` and committed.
- Run the project's pre-commit gate (tests, lint, format) before
  `agentrail complete`, not after.
- If you discover unplanned work, prefer `agentrail insert` / `agentrail add`
  over silently doing it inside another step.

## CRITICAL: Agentrail session protocol (follow exactly)

Every session follows this sequence. Do not skip steps, do not reorder.

### 1. START — `agentrail next`
First thing in the session. Read the output carefully: it tells you the
current step number, prompt, skill docs, and past trajectories. If `next`
exits non-zero, the saga is complete or absent — do not invent work.

### 2. BEGIN — `agentrail begin`
Run immediately after reading `next` output. This transitions the step from
Pending to InProgress so the recorded history matches what actually
happened.

### 3. WORK
Do what the step prompt says. Do NOT ask the user "want me to proceed?" or
"shall I start?" — the step prompt IS your instruction. Execute it.

### 4. COMMIT
Commit your code changes with git BEFORE running `agentrail complete`.
The commit recorded into the step's `commits` field comes from `HEAD` at
the moment of `complete`, so the commit must land first.

### 5. COMPLETE — `agentrail complete`
```
agentrail complete --summary "what you accomplished" \
  --reward 1 \
  --actions "tools and approach used"
```
On failure: `--reward -1 --failure-mode "what went wrong"`.
On final step: add `--done`.

### 6. STOP
After `complete`, do NOT make further code changes. Anything after
`complete` is untracked and invisible to the next session. If you see more
work to do, it belongs in the NEXT step, not this one.

## Agentrail metadata discipline

When using agentrail, changes to `.agentrail/` files are first-class project
changes — the same as application source code. They must be committed, and
should be pushed before you hand off.

Before running `agentrail complete`:

1. `git status` — confirm `.agentrail/` files are tracked, not just present.
   Untracked files in `.agentrail/` mean the next session will not see them.
2. Stage and commit source changes and `.agentrail/` metadata together. The
   commit recorded into the step's `commits` field comes from `HEAD` at the
   moment of `agentrail complete`, so the commit must happen *first*.
3. Run `agentrail complete` after the commit lands.
4. Push the branch (or note the unpushed branch state in your handoff).

This is the most common agentrail failure mode: agents do the work, commit
the source, and forget the `.agentrail/` files. The result is a saga whose
recorded history disagrees with git history, which `agentrail audit` will
flag — but only after the damage is done.

### What's hand-editable in `.agentrail/`

Three categories of files live here, and the rules differ:

- **Append-only saga state** — `saga.toml`, `step.toml`, `plan.md`, session
  JSONLs under `sessions/`, trajectory JSONs under `trajectories/`, and
  anything under `.agentrail-archive/`. **Never hand-edit or delete these.**
  They are written by agentrail commands and represent the durable saga
  record; hand-editing desyncs the saga from git history and from prior
  session memory. A direct `rm` on untracked files is unrecoverable.
- **Regenerated state** — `instruction-lock.toml`. Don't hand-edit; it is
  rewritten on every `agentrail instructions apply`, so any local changes
  are overwritten silently.
- **User config** — `instruction-profile.toml`. This is normal user-edited
  config, like `.gitconfig` or a `package.json`. Hand-edit it freely, or
  use `agentrail instructions profile *` subcommands to mutate via
  commands (which validate field values and surface typos).

## Recovery: detecting and repairing saga/git drift

The saga is a record of git history. When the two diverge — agent forgets
to commit `.agentrail/`, a step is reverted, files are renamed by hand —
agentrail provides two recovery tools.

### `agentrail audit`

Compares first-parent git history against saga steps and reports gaps.
Default output is a markdown report; `--emit-commands` prints a shell
script of `agentrail add` lines pre-seeded from commit subjects:

```bash
agentrail audit                    # human-readable report
agentrail audit --emit-commands    # draft script (review before running)
agentrail audit --since HEAD~50    # limit scope
```

The emitted script is a draft — slugs and prompts come from commit
subjects and usually need rewording. Review and edit before executing.

### `agentrail snapshot` (belt-and-suspenders)

Captures `.agentrail/` (and `.agentrail-archive/` if present) into a real
git commit under `refs/agentrail/snapshots/<timestamp>`. The blobs are
reachable, survive `git gc`, and can be restored with a normal git
command:

```bash
agentrail snapshot                 # take a snapshot now
agentrail snapshot --list          # list existing refs
git restore --source=<ref> -- .agentrail .agentrail-archive
```

Run a snapshot before risky agent operations or after creating files
you haven't yet staged. It does NOT replace normal git tracking — it is
a safety net for what is not yet committed.

## Git hygiene

- Never amend a commit that has already been pushed to a shared branch.
- Never use `--no-verify` to skip pre-commit hooks unless explicitly told to.
  If a hook fails, fix the underlying issue.
- Prefer naming files explicitly (`git add path/to/file`) over `git add -A`,
  to avoid sweeping in unintended files (secrets, local scratch, etc.).
- Resolve merge conflicts; do not discard changes by default.

Instructions for AI coding agents (Claude Code, opencode, Cursor, etc.)
working in this repository. This project uses **agentrail** to keep
multi-session agent work on track. Follow these rules exactly.

Rename or copy this file to whatever your agent reads (`AGENTS.md`,
`CLAUDE.md`, `.cursorrules`, etc.) — the content is the same.

---

## The one-paragraph summary

This project uses agentrail to record work as a sequence of **steps** in a
**saga**. Each session you run does exactly one step: read the step prompt
with `agentrail next`, start it with `agentrail begin`, do the work, commit
your changes with git, and close the step with `agentrail complete`. Then
stop — the next step is for the next session. The `.agentrail/` directory
is the durable record and must be tracked in git like source code.

## The session protocol (follow exactly)

### 1. START — read your instructions

```bash
agentrail next
```

This prints the current step's prompt, relevant context files, skill
documents, and past successful trajectories for this task type. **Read
the entire output carefully.** It is the instruction for this session.

If `agentrail next` exits with no current step, the saga is paused or
complete — stop and ask the user what to do. Do not invent work.

### 2. BEGIN — transition the step

```bash
agentrail begin
```

This marks the step as `in-progress`. Required before doing work.

### 3. WORK — do exactly what the step prompt says

- Do not ask the user "want me to proceed?" or "shall I start?". The
  step prompt **is** your instruction. Execute it.
- Do not expand scope. If you notice other problems, note them for a
  future step — do not silently fix them in this one.
- Stay within the files the step prompt references. If you need to touch
  something outside that scope, pause and ask.

### 4. COMMIT — commit your work with git

```bash
git add <files>
git commit -m "<clear message>"
```

**This must happen before `agentrail complete`.** `agentrail complete`
captures the current `HEAD` commit hash into the step's `commits` field,
which is how future `agentrail audit` runs link the step back to its
commit. If you complete before committing, the linkage is wrong.

Include `.agentrail/` files you touched in the commit — they are part of
the record.

### 5. COMPLETE — close the step

```bash
agentrail complete \
  --summary "what you accomplished in one or two sentences" \
  --reward 1 \
  --actions "tools and approach used"
```

Flags:
- `--reward 1` on success, `--reward -1 --failure-mode "<what-went-wrong>"`
  on failure. Reward is used for trajectory recording so future sessions
  can learn from what worked.
- Add `--done` if this was the last step of the saga.
- Use `--next-slug` and `--next-prompt` to define the next step if you
  know what it should be; otherwise the human will plan it.

### 6. STOP — do not continue
